items.title: Eddie Dawson Interview, 1961-06-28
items.q: I was playing and Manuel Perez was getting all that work out there at Millenboy when Gossum, a fella called Gossum was giving them picnics out there.

ctx.x: You were speaking about Freddie Kepard earlier. What kind of a style? Was he any different to the other trumpet players? No, no.

He played that Dixieland and jazz trumpet just like the rest of them. Yeah. They all have to play that same way, you see, when you play the trumpet. Because when you get in a band, if you're playing trumpet in a band like they was playing then, you'd have to play that style, you know? The only difference was some fellas could play in brass band music and they couldn't play dance music, you see. That's the two different types of music, you see. When there's a straight and a jazz the other way to dance and music,…

Well, I read Piku told us something about playing out there too with Manuel Perez. Oh, yeah, yeah. I played with Piku out there too. Piku said he remembers the same time when Freddie picked up the cornet sometime.

items.title: Eddie Dawson Interview, 1959-08-11
items.q: And Manuel Perez was playing trumpet. And we had the same fella Jimmy Pollard playing violin too... We used to play at Millenburg for picnics out there.

ctx.x: Oh, yeah. He told that funny story about him being on the Smoky Mary. Tell us about it.

We used to play at Millenburg for picnics out there. Those were only picnics. And Sidney Bechet, he was playing clarinet with us, you see. And well, and Manuel Perez was playing trumpet. And we had the same fella Jimmy Pollard playing violin too. He used to play with his two over there. And we'd play them picnics. Cause we used to take a man when needed a man on the picnic. We'd have extra man when needed, you see. And Sidney Bechet would get on that old Smoky Mary, you know, that running out the Millenburg and…
Well, speaking of that term Dixieland, I never did ask fast either. When the word jazz began being used here in New Orleans, can you remember?
